text.en: Raju saw the expression 3x + 5 on the board. "What is its value when x is 2?" asked his teacher.

A polynomial is an expression with whole-number powers of a variable, named by degree as linear, quadratic or cubic, and by terms as monomial, binomial or trinomial. The value of a polynomial is found by putting a number for the variable, and a zero of the polynomial is a value that makes it 0.
The remainder theorem says that when p(x) is divided by (x - a), the remainder is p(a). The factor theorem says that (x - a) is a factor of p(x) if and only if p(a) = 0. Algebraic identities such as (a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2, (a - b)^2 and a^2 - b^2 = (a + b)(a - b) help us expand and factorise.
Factorisation writes a polynomial as a product, by identities or by splitting the middle term of a quadratic trinomial. Use polynomial long division to divide by a nonzero polynomial. Synthetic division is a useful shortcut when the divisor has the form x minus a. The greatest common divisor is a common factor of greatest degree. One linear equation in two variables can have many ordered-pair solutions.

Read three x squared minus two x plus five as three terms with coefficients three, minus two and five. The highest exponent with a nonzero coefficient is two, so this is quadratic.
A term like x to the power minus one is one divided by x. Its exponent is negative, so an expression with that term is outside the class of polynomials in x.
A nonzero constant, such as seven, has degree zero. After cancellation, x minus x is the zero polynomial, whose degree is left undefined here.
Evaluate three x squared minus two x plus five at negative two. Put brackets around negative two before squaring, so its square is positive four.
Two polynomials can have the same value at one input and different values elsewhere. A zero of one polynomial simply marks a particular input where that expression equals zero.

board.text: Value at one input is not a polynomial identity

text.en: When a divisor is x plus two, write it as x minus negative two. The number to substitute in the remainder theorem is negative two.
For polynomial x squared plus three x plus two, substitute negative two. Four minus six plus two gives zero, so x plus two divides the polynomial with no remainder.
A square of side a plus b can be divided into a square of side a, a square of side b and two rectangles of sides a and b. Both rectangles contribute to the middle term.
In x squared minus six x plus nine, the last term is the square of three and the middle term is minus two times x times three. The expression is the square of x minus three.
Compare x squared minus nine with the last square. Here the middle term is absent, and we subtract one square from another. The factor pair is x plus three and x minus three.
First look for a shared factor in each term. In six x squared plus nine x, both terms share three x. Dividing the terms by three x leaves two x and three in brackets.
To factor two x squared plus seven x plus three, split seven x into six x and x. The new coefficients add to seven and multiply to six, the product of the leading and constant coefficients.
Group the first two terms and the last two. They become two x times x plus three, and one times x plus three. Factor out the shared bracket.
For polynomial long division, divide the leading term first, multiply by the whole divisor and subtract. Repeat until the remainder degree is smaller than the divisor degree.
Check a division by multiplying the divisor and quotient, then adding the remainder. For x squared plus one divided by x minus one, the quotient is x plus one and the remainder is two.

For that same linear divisor, synthetic division uses one. Use coefficients one, zero and one, including the missing x term. Bring down, multiply and add to get quotient coefficients one, one and remainder two.
To find a greatest common divisor by factoring, compare each shared factor and its multiplicity. For two factors shared only once, use that common factor only once.

board.text: GCD uses the smaller multiplicity of each shared factor

text.en: For x squared minus nine and x squared minus six x plus nine, the only shared linear factor is x minus three. The first polynomial contains it just once.
The equation x plus y equals seven has many ordered pairs. Four comma three and five comma two both work. Plotting all its solutions gives a straight line.

board.text: x + y = 7 has a line of solutions

text.en: A second condition says x minus y equals one. An ordered pair solving the system must satisfy both conditions, so its point appears on both lines.

board.text: Both equations must hold at the crossing

text.en: Add those two equations. The y terms cancel and two x equals eight. Then x is four, and substitution into the first equation gives y equals three.
Check both equations using four comma three. If the x and y values satisfy one equation but fail the other, the pair is a solution of one line rather than the system.

problem.en: Find a pair that satisfies x + y = 7 and x − y = 1.

text.en: Add the equations to get two x equals eight.

why.en: One positive y and one negative y cancel.

text.en: Divide by two to find x equals four. Then substitute into the first equation to get y equals three.
Check four minus three as well.

why.en: It equals one, so the ordered pair satisfies both equations.
